title: Your crypto cost per coin is the average, not the last price.
made_by: 엔진/find.py 2026-11-04 · 신호 ['s1ea3491b', 'sb7e63a60'] · 퍼스나 The headline-chasing new holder

fact.thing: extra tax from using the last purchase price instead of the average cost
fact.box: Non-registered crypto holdings, Ontario resident, 2026 taxable income $58,523 to $94,907
fact.claim: For identical properties, the CRA says your cost per unit (ACB) is the total cost of all your purchases divided by the number of units you own. Not your last purchase price. Worked example: buy 3 coins at $9,000, $7,000 and $5,000, for an average cost of $7,000 each. Then sell all 3 for $10,000 each. The correct gain is $9,000, but using the $5,000 last price makes it $15,000. Half of a capital gain is taxable, and at Ontario's 2026 combined rate of 29.65% for this income range, the $6,000 overstated gain costs about $890 in extra tax. These prices are made up for illustration. The result depends on your real prices, your income and the order you bought in, and if your last purchase was your most expensive one, the same mistake makes you underpay instead.

felt.how: tax using last price vs tax using average cost, on 3 coins sold for $30,000

sources.label: CRA T4037 CAPITAL GAINS 2025
sources.what: You may buy and sell several identical properties at different prices over a period of time. If you do this, you have to calculate the average cost of each property in the group at the time of each purchase to determine your ACB. Dispositions of identical properties do not affect the ACB.

sources.label: CRA T4037 CAPITAL GAINS 2025
sources.what: The average cost is calculated by dividing the total cost of identical properties purchased (this is usually the cost of the property plus any expenses involved in acquiring it) by the total number of identical properties owned.

sources.label: CRA GUIDE FOR CRYPTOCURRENCY USERS
sources.what: If you have disposed of a crypto-asset on account of capital, you must include half of your capital gains (known as taxable capital gains) in your income for the year.

plain.what: If you buy the same coin at different prices, the CRA wants you to use your average cost per coin, not the price you paid last time. Say you bought 3 bitcoins at $9,000, $7,000 and $5,000, then sold all 3 for $10,000 each. The average cost is $7,000 a coin, so your gain is $9,000 — but using the last price of $5,000 makes the gain look like $15,000.
plain.so_what: That mistake overstates your gain by $6,000, and in Ontario in 2026 on income between $58,523 and $94,907, it means about $890 more tax than you owed.
plain.do: Open your tax app today and write down which cost per coin it uses: your last buy, or the average.
